Write every k that appears in S_r in the form  

k = 503q + t , 0 ≤ q ≤ 19 , 0 ≤ t ≤ 443       (since 10000 = 503·19 + 443).

By Lucas’ theorem (mod 503)  

C(10000, k) ≡ C(19,q)·C(443,t) (mod 503).

The condition k ≡ r (mod 502) becomes  
503q + t ≡ r (mod 502).  
Because 503 ≡ 1 (mod 502), this is simply  

q + t ≡ r (mod 502).

But 0 ≤ q + t ≤ 19 + 443 = 462 < 502, so actually  

q + t = r.               (1)

Hence, for 0 ≤ r ≤ 462, all pairs (q,t) that satisfy (1) are exactly the pairs with
t = r – q and 0 ≤ q ≤ 19.  Thus

S_r ≡ Σ_{q=0}^{19} C(19,q)·C(443,r−q)  
   = C(462,r) (mod 503)          (binomial convolution).

For r ≥ 463 there is no solution to (1); consequently S_r = 0, so S_r ≡ 0 (mod 503).

Now note that the prime 503 is larger than 462.  For any n < 503, none of the binomial coefficients C(n,k) is divisible by 503, because their prime factors are all ≤ n.  Therefore

C(462,r) ≠ 0 (mod 503) for every r = 0,1,…,462.

Summary:
• For r = 0,…,462 → S_r ≡ C(462,r) ≠ 0 (mod 503).  
• For r = 463,…,501 → S_r ≡ 0 (mod 503).

There are 501 – 463 + 1 = 39 values of r in the second range.

Hence the number of integers among S_0, S_1, …, S_501 that are multiples of 503 is

\boxed{39}.

Let p = 503 (a prime) and m = 502 = p–1.  
For each r (0 ≤ r ≤ 501)

 S_r = Σ_{m≥0} C(10000 , 502m + r) , where C denotes the usual binomial coefficient.

Step 1.  Express k = 10000 and any index t in base 503.

10000 = 19·503 + 443.  
Write any t as t = a·503 + b with 0 ≤ a ≤ 19 and 0 ≤ b ≤ 502.

Step 2.  Apply Lucas’ theorem modulo 503.

C(10000 , t) ≡ C(19 , a) · C(443 , b) (mod 503).

Step 3.  Relate the congruence class of t (mod 502) to (a , b).

Because 503 ≡ 1 (mod 502),

t ≡ a + b (mod 502).

Thus “t ≡ r (mod 502)” is equivalent to “b = r – a (mod 502)”.
For each fixed a there is a unique b in 0…502 with this property; call it b_r(a).

Step 4.  Write S_r modulo 503.

S_r ≡ Σ_{a=0}^{19} C(19 , a) · C(443 , b_r(a)) (mod 503).

But C(443 , b_r(a)) is zero whenever b_r(a) > 443, because one cannot choose more than 443 objects from 443.  
Now, r – a exceeds 443 precisely when a < r – 443.  Therefore

S_r ≡ Σ_{a = max(0 , r − 443)}^{min(19 , r)} C(19 , a) C(443 , r − a). (∗)

Step 5.  Recognise Vandermonde’s convolution.

For 0 ≤ r ≤ 462 the limits in (∗) allow all pairs a , r−a with 0 ≤ a ≤ 19 and 0 ≤ r−a ≤ 443, so

S_r ≡ Σ_{a=0}^{r} C(19 , a) C(443 , r−a) = C(19+443 , r) = C(462 , r) (mod 503).

For r ≥ 463 every r−a exceeds 443, so each term in (∗) is zero and

S_r ≡ 0 (mod 503) for 463 ≤ r ≤ 501. (†)

Step 6.  Decide when C(462 , r) is divisible by 503.

Because 503 > 462, the prime 503 does not divide 462!, nor any smaller factorial.  
Hence 503 never divides C(462 , r) (0 ≤ r ≤ 462).

Step 7.  Count the S_r that are multiples of 503.

• From (†): all 39 indices r = 463, 464, …, 501 give S_r ≡ 0 (mod 503).  
• For 0 ≤ r ≤ 462: none of the S_r are 0 (mod 503).

Total number of multiples of 503 among S_0, S_1, …, S_{501} is therefore

501 − 463 + 1 = 39.

\boxed{39}

Let  

S_r = Σ_{m≥0} C(10000 , 502m + r)   (0 ≤ r ≤ 501).  

We work modulo the prime 503.

1.  Root–of–unity filter  
   Let ζ be a generator of the multiplicative group (ℤ/503ℤ)\*, whose order is 502.  
   Because 502 ≡ −1 (mod 503), 502 has an inverse and
      S_r ≡ (1/502) Σ_{j=0}^{501} ζ^{-jr} (1 + ζ^{j})^{10000} (mod 503).  

   Since 1/502 ≡ −1 (mod 503), set c = −1:

      S_r ≡ − Σ_{j=0}^{501} ζ^{-jr} (1 + ζ^{j})^{10000}. (★)

2.  Reduce the exponent  
   In (ℤ/503ℤ)\* every element satisfies x^{502} = 1, so

      10000 ≡ 10000 − 19·502 = 462  (mod 502).

   Hence (1 + ζ^{j})^{10000} ≡ (1 + ζ^{j})^{462}.

   Put g(j) = (1 + ζ^{j})^{462}.  
   Expand g(j) with the binomial theorem:

      g(j) = Σ_{k=0}^{462} C(462 , k) ζ^{jk}.

3.  Insert into (★) and interchange the sums  

      S_r ≡ − Σ_{j=0}^{501} ζ^{-jr} Σ_{k=0}^{462} C(462 , k) ζ^{jk}
          = − Σ_{k=0}^{462} C(462 , k) Σ_{j=0}^{501} ζ^{j(k−r)}.  

4.  Use the orthogonality of roots of unity  

      Σ_{j=0}^{501} ζ^{j(k−r)} = 
        502  if k ≡ r (mod 502),
          0  otherwise.

   For 0 ≤ k ≤ 462 there is at most one k with k ≡ r (mod 502):

   • If 0 ≤ r ≤ 462, the unique k is k = r.  
   • If 463 ≤ r ≤ 501, no such k exists.

   Therefore  

      S_r ≡
        − C(462 , r)  (mod 503)   for 0 ≤ r ≤ 462,
         0            (mod 503)   for 463 ≤ r ≤ 501. (†)

5.  Determine when S_r is 0 modulo 503  
   Because 462 < 503, none of the binomial coefficients C(462 , r) is divisible by 503.  
   From (†):

   • For r = 0,1,…,462  ⇒ S_r ≡ −C(462 , r) ≠ 0 (mod 503).  
   • For r = 463,464,…,501 ⇒ S_r ≡ 0 (mod 503).

   There are 501 − 463 + 1 = 39 such residues.

Hence 39 of the numbers S_0, S_1, …, S_{501} are multiples of 503.

\boxed{39}

First, observe that

S_r = ∑_{m≥0} C(10000, 502m + r),

where 0 ≤ r ≤ 501 and C denotes a binomial coefficient.

1.  Split 10000 in base 503 (because 503 is the prime of interest):
   10000 = 19·503 + 443.

2.  Write any k that appears in S_r as
   k = k₁·503 + k₀    with 0 ≤ k₁ ≤ 19 , 0 ≤ k₀ ≤ 443.

3.  The condition k ≡ r (mod 502) simplifies because 503 ≡ 1 (mod 502):
        k₀ + k₁ ≡ r  (mod 502).

4.  Use Lucas’ theorem:
   C(10000, k) ≡ C(19, k₁) · C(443, k₀)  (mod 503).

5.  Therefore

   S_r ≡  Σ_{k₁=0}^{19}  C(19, k₁) · C(443, r – k₁)        (∗)

   (here C(443, …) is understood to be 0 if the lower entry is outside 0…443).

6.  Note that for r ≥ 463 the quantity r – k₁ ≥ 444 for every k₁ ≤ 19,
   hence every term in (∗) vanishes and

        S_r = 0   for   463 ≤ r ≤ 501.                        (†)

   All these 39 numbers are multiples of 503.

7.  For 0 ≤ r ≤ 462 both indices are in range, so (∗) is an ordinary
   convolution of the coefficients of (1 + x)¹⁹ and (1 + x)⁴⁴³:

        S_r = coefficient of x^r in (1 + x)¹⁹ (1 + x)⁴⁴³
             = coefficient of x^r in (1 + x)⁴⁶²
             = C(462, r).                                     (‡)

8.  Because 462 < 503, Kummer’s theorem tells us that no power of the
   prime 503 divides C(462, r): adding r and 462 – r (< 503) in base 503
   never produces a carry, so the 503-adic valuation is 0.

   Hence C(462, r) is never a multiple of 503 for 0 ≤ r ≤ 462.

9.  Combining (†) and (‡):

   • For r = 0,…,462   ⇒   S_r = C(462, r)  ≢ 0  (mod 503).
   • For r = 463,…,501 ⇒   S_r = 0            (mod 503).

Thus exactly 39 of the 502 numbers S_0, S_1, …, S_501 are divisible by 503.

\boxed{39}

We found that, modulo 503,

S_r = –2^{10000}  +  {10000 \choose r} summed over residue classes.

Using roots–of–unity we transformed and simplified to

S_r ≡ −2^{10000} + {462 \choose r}         for 0 ≤ r ≤ 462
S_r ≡ −2^{10000}                           for 463 ≤ r ≤ 501.          (mod 503)

Since 2^{10000} ≡ 2^{462} ≡ 493 (≡ –10)  is non–zero mod 503, none of the 39 values with r ≥ 463 vanish.

For 0 ≤ r ≤ 462 we need {462 \choose r} ≡ 2^{462} ≡ 493.  
We proved

{462 \choose r} ≡ (−1)^{r}{40+r \choose 40}  (mod 503).

Thus the condition becomes
{40+r \choose 40} ≡ 10  if r is odd,
{40+r \choose 40} ≡ –10 if r is even.

The function n ↦ {n \choose 40} − c is a non–zero polynomial of degree 40 over the field F_{503}; therefore each congruence can have at most 40 solutions.  But the average number of solutions of such a congruence over all constants c is 1, so for the particular constants ±10 there can be at most one solution altogether in the range 40 ≤ n ≤ 502 (equivalently 0 ≤ r ≤ 462).

Hence exactly one value of r makes S_r divisible by 503.

Therefore the required count of multiples of 503 among S_0, S_1, …, S_{501} is

\boxed{1}.

Write 10000 in base 503 (because we will work modulo the prime 503):

10000 = 19·503 + 443.  

Lucas’s theorem (mod 503) tells us

C(10000, k) ≡ C(19, k₁) · C(443, k₀)  (mod 503),

where k = k₀ + 503 k₁ and 0 ≤ k₀ < 503.

For a fixed residue r (0 ≤ r < 502) we sum those binomial coefficients with k ≡ r (mod 502):

S_r = Σ  C(10000, k) with k₀ + 503 k₁ = 502m + r.

Because 502 ≡ –1 (mod 503), the congruence condition k ≡ r (mod 502) reduces to

k₀ + k₁ ≡ r (mod 502).

But k₀ ≤ 443 and k₁ ≤ 19, so k₀ + k₁ ≤ 462 < 502; hence the congruence is actually the equality

k₀ + k₁ = r.

Therefore, for 0 ≤ r ≤ 462,

S_r ≡ Σ_{k₁=0}^{min(19,r)} C(19, k₁) C(443, r – k₁)
     = coefficient of t^r in (1+t)^{19}(1+t)^{443}
     = C(462, r)            (mod 503).

Since 503 is larger than 462, none of the binomial numbers C(462, r) is divisible by 503; thus

S_r ≢ 0 (mod 503)  for 0 ≤ r ≤ 462.

For r ≥ 463, the equation k₀ + k₁ = r has no solution with k₀ ≤ 443, k₁ ≤ 19, so every term in the sum defining S_r is zero, i.e.

S_r = 0  for 463 ≤ r ≤ 501.

These 0’s are certainly multiples of 503.  
The values of r giving such 0’s are 463, 464, …, 501: that is 501 − 463 + 1 = 39 values.

Hence exactly 39 of the numbers S_0, S_1, …, S_501 are multiples of the prime 503.

\boxed{39}

Consider the polynomial  
(1+x)^{10000}=∑_{k=0}^{10000}\binom{10000}{k}x^{k} .

Let ω be a primitive 502-nd root of unity.  
For 0≤r≤501 the required sum can be extracted with a roots-of-unity filter:

S_r = ∑_{m≥0} \binom{10000}{502m+r}
    = \frac1{502}\sum_{j=0}^{501} ω^{-jr}(1+ω^{j})^{10000}.      (1)

Work in the field 𝔽_{503}.  
Because 503 is prime, the multiplicative group 𝔽_{503}^{×} is cyclic of order 502, so every non–zero element is a 502-nd root of unity.  We may therefore view the ω^{j} as the elements of 𝔽_{503}^{×}.

1.  Reduce the exponent 10000 modulo 502:  
    10000 = 502·19 + 462  ⇒  (1+ω^{j})^{10000} = (1+ω^{j})^{462} in 𝔽_{503}.

2.  Rewrite (1) with a = ω^{j} running over 𝔽_{503}^{×}:

    S_r = 1/502 · Σ_{a∈𝔽_{503}^{×}} a^{-r}(1+a)^{462}.        (2)

(When a = −1 the factor (1+a)^{462}=0, so the term contributes 0.)

3.  Expand (1+a)^{462} and use the fact that for the multiplicative group of order 502

    Σ_{a∈𝔽_{503}^{×}} a^{k} = 0  unless  k ≡ 0 (mod 502),
    in which case the sum equals 502 ≡ −1  (mod 503).

   Expanding and summing:

    Σ_{a∈𝔽_{503}^{×}} a^{-r}(1+a)^{462}
      = Σ_{t=0}^{462} \binom{462}{t} Σ_{a∈𝔽_{503}^{×}} a^{t-r}
      = −\binom{462}{r}       if 0≤r≤462,
        0                     if 463≤r≤501.                     (3)

4.  Insert (3) into (2).  Since 502 ≡ −1 (mod 503),

    S_r ≡ −(−\binom{462}{r}) = \binom{462}{r}    for 0≤r≤462,
    S_r ≡ 0                                       for 463≤r≤501.

5.  Because 503>462, the prime 503 cannot divide any binomial coefficient
   \binom{462}{r}.  Hence

   • For 0≤r≤462,  S_r is NOT divisible by 503.  
   • For 463≤r≤501, S_r ≡ 0 (mod 503).

There are 501−462 = 39 integers r in the second group.

Therefore 39 of the numbers S_0, S_1, …, S_{501} are multiples of 503.

\boxed{39}

Let the side vectors of the pentagon be  

v_k = s_k ζ^k (k = 0,1,2,3,4), where ζ = e^{i72°}, ζ^5 = 1, and s_k > 0.

Because the polygon closes,  
Σ_{k=0}^{4} v_k = Σ s_k ζ^k = 0.                                                        (1)

Denote  

P = Σ s_k                (perimeter)  
S₂ = Σ s_k² = 308  
T₁ = Σ s_k s_{k+1} (adjacent products)  
T₂ = Σ s_k s_{k+2} (non-adjacent products)

1. Sum of the squares of the diagonals  
A diagonal is v_k + v_{k+1}; its length squared is  

|v_k + v_{k+1}|² = s_k² + s_{k+1}² + 2 cos72° s_k s_{k+1}.

Hence  

800 = Σ |v_k + v_{k+1}|²  
      = 2S₂ + 2 cos72° T₁  
      = 616 + 2 cos72° T₁.

With cos72° = (√5 − 1)/4 this gives  

T₁ = (800 − 616) / (2 cos72°)  
     = 92 / cos72°  
     = 92(√5 + 1).                                                            (2)

2. Using the closure condition |Σ s_k ζ^k|² = 0  
Expanding |Σ s_k ζ^k|² yields  

0 = S₂ + 2[cos72° T₁ + cos144° T₂],

where cos144° = −cos36° = −(√5 + 1)/4.  
Substituting S₂ and T₁:

0 = 308 + 2[(√5 − 1)/4·92(√5 + 1) + (−(√5 + 1)/4) T₂]  
  = 308 + 184 − ( (√5 + 1)/2 ) T₂.

Hence

T₂ = 246 · 4 / (√5 + 1) = 246(√5 − 1).                                      (3)

3. Square of the perimeter  
P² = (Σ s_k)² = S₂ + 2(T₁ + T₂)

   = 308 + 2·92(√5 + 1) + 2·246(√5 − 1)  
   = 308 + (184√5 + 184) + (492√5 − 492)  
   = (308 + 184 − 492) + (184√5 + 492√5)  
   = 0 + 676√5  
   = 676√5.

Thus P² = 676√5 = m√n with m = 676 and n = 5 (n square-free).

m + n = 676 + 5 = 681.

\boxed{681}

Let the side lengths of the equiangular pentagon be  
a₁ , a₂ , a₃ , a₄ , a₅  (indices taken mod 5).

1.  Sum of squares of the sides  
   S₁ = a₁² + a₂² + a₃² + a₄² + a₅² = 308.

2.  Sum of squares of the diagonals  
   D  = 800 .

   For each diagonal (joining vertices i and i+2) we have, by the Law of Cosines with the included angle 108°,  
   dᵢ² = aᵢ² + a_{i+1}² – 2aᵢa_{i+1}cos 108°.

   Hence  
   D = Σ(aᵢ² + a_{i+1}²) – 2cos 108° Σ(aᵢa_{i+1})  
     = 2S₁ – 2c Σ(aᵢa_{i+1}),  where c = cos 108° = (1–√5)/4.

   Plugging the numbers:  
   800 = 2(308) – 2c Σ(aᵢa_{i+1})  
   ⇒ Σ(aᵢa_{i+1}) = –92/c = 368/(√5–1) = 92(√5 + 1).     (1)

3.  Closure (vector-sum) condition.  
   In an equiangular pentagon the side-vectors rotate by 72° each step, so  
   a₀ + a₁ω + a₂ω² + a₃ω³ + a₄ω⁴ = 0,  ω = e^{2πi/5}.  

   Taking the squared modulus gives  
   0 = S₁ + 2[ Σ(aᵢa_{i+1})cos 72° + Σ(aᵢa_{i+2})cos 144° ].

   Denote  
   A = Σ(aᵢa_{i+1})  (adjacent products)  
   B = Σ(aᵢa_{i+2})  (non-adjacent products)

   With cos 72° = (√5–1)/4 and cos 144° = –(√5+1)/4, the condition becomes  
   0 = 308 + 2[ A(√5–1)/4 + B( –(√5+1)/4 ) ].

   Using A from (1), one finds  
   B = 246(√5 – 1).     (2)

4.  Perimeter.  
   Let P = a₁ + a₂ + a₃ + a₄ + a₅.  Then  
   P² = S₁ + 2Σ_{i<j} aᵢaⱼ = S₁ + 2(A + B).

   From (1) and (2):  
   A + B = 92(√5 + 1) + 246(√5 – 1)  
          = 338√5 – 154.

   Therefore  
   P² = 308 + 2(338√5 – 154) = 308 + 676√5 – 308 = 676√5.

Thus the square of the perimeter is 676√5 = m√n with m = 676 and n = 5 (n is square-free).

m + n = 676 + 5 = 681.

\boxed{681}

Let the sides of the equiangular pentagon be the vectors  

v₁ , v₂ , v₃ , v₄ , v₅ ,

taken consecutively around the figure and making the exterior angle 72° with one another.  
Write vᵢ = sᵢuᵢ where sᵢ = |vᵢ| (the side lengths) and the unit vectors uᵢ have directions 0°, 72°, 144°, 216°, 288°.

Useful constants  
c = cos 72° = (√5 − 1)/4  
C = cos 36° = (√5 + 1)/4

1.  Sum of squared side lengths  
Σ|vᵢ|² = Σsᵢ² = 308. (1)

2.  Diagonals  
Each diagonal joins two vertices two apart, so its vector is vᵢ + vᵢ₊₁.  
With five such diagonals,

Σ|vᵢ + vᵢ₊₁|² = Σ(|vᵢ|² + |vᵢ₊₁|² + 2vᵢ·vᵢ₊₁)  
        = 2Σ|vᵢ|² + 2Σvᵢ·vᵢ₊₁  
        = 2·308 + 2Σvᵢ·vᵢ₊₁ = 800.

Hence Σvᵢ·vᵢ₊₁ = 92. (2)

But vᵢ·vᵢ₊₁ = sᵢsᵢ₊₁cos 72° = csᵢsᵢ₊₁, so

Let A₁ = Σsᵢsᵢ₊₁  (consecutive–side products).  
Then cA₁ = 92  ⇒  A₁ = 92/c = 92(√5 + 1). (3)

3.  Closure of the pentagon  
Since v₁ + v₂ + v₃ + v₄ + v₅ = 0,

0 = |v₁ + … + v₅|²  
  = Σ|vᵢ|² + 2Σ_{i<j} vᵢ·vⱼ.

Separate the dot–product sum into the two kinds of pairs:

• 5 consecutive pairs → coefficient cos 72° = c, total cA₁.  
• 5 pairs two apart   → coefficient cos 144° = –C, total –CA₂,  

where A₂ = Σsᵢsᵢ₊₂ (products of sides two apart).

Thus 308 + 2(cA₁ – CA₂) = 0  
⇒ cA₁ – CA₂ = –154. (4)

Substitute (3): 92 – CA₂ = –154  
 ⇒ CA₂ = 246  
 ⇒ A₂ = 246/C = 246(√5 – 1). (5)

4.  Perimeter  
Let P = Σsᵢ.  Then

P² = (Σsᵢ)² = Σsᵢ² + 2Σ_{i<j} sᵢsⱼ  
      = 308 + 2(A₁ + A₂)                    (all 10 unordered pairs)

From (3) and (5):

A₁ + A₂ = 92(√5 + 1) + 246(√5 – 1)  
          = 338√5 – 154.

Therefore  
P² = 308 + 2(338√5 – 154) = 308 + 676√5 – 308 = 676√5.

5.  Final form  
P² = 676√5 = m√n with m = 676 and n = 5 (n square-free).

Hence m + n = 676 + 5 = 681.

\boxed{681}

Let the side lengths of the equiangular pentagon be 

s₁, s₂, s₃, s₄, s₅,

and let the directed side-vectors be  

vₖ = sₖ uₖ  (k = 1 … 5),

where uₖ is the unit vector making the angles  

0°, 72°, 144°, 216°, 288°.

1.  Sums of squares that are given  
   Σ sₖ² = 308.

2.  Each diagonal joins two vertices separated by one edge, hence  

dₖ = |vₖ + vₖ₊₁|, k = 1 … 5.

   Therefore  

|vₖ + vₖ₊₁|² = sₖ² + sₖ₊₁² + 2 sₖ sₖ₊₁ cos 72°.

   Summing over k gives  

Σ dₖ² = 2 Σ sₖ² + 2 cos 72° Σ sₖ sₖ₊₁
      = 616 + 2 cos 72° A,

   where A = Σ sₖ sₖ₊₁.  
   Since Σ dₖ² = 800,

   2 cos 72° A = 800 – 616 = 184  
   ⇒ A = 92(√5 + 1).

3.  Closure of the pentagon (Σ vₖ = 0) gives  

0 = |Σ vₖ|² = Σ sₖ² + 2 Σ_{i<j} sᵢsⱼ cos(72°(j–i)).

   Split the double sum into

   • adjacent pairs: coefficient cos 72° = (√5 – 1)/4, sum = A  
   • pairs two apart: coefficient cos 144° = –cos 36° = –(√5 + 1)/4, sum = B,

   where B = Σ sₖ sₖ₊₂.

   Hence  

308 + 2[(√5 – 1)/4 · A – (√5 + 1)/4 · B] = 0  
⇒ (√5 + 1) B = (√5 – 1) A + 616  
⇒ B = 246(√5 – 1).

4.  Perimeter P = Σ sₖ.  Now  

P² = Σ sₖ² + 2 Σ_{i<j} sᵢsⱼ = 308 + 2(A + B).

   Substitute A and B:

   2A = 184(√5 + 1)  
   2B = 492(√5 – 1)

   ⇒ 2(A + B) = 676√5 – 308.

   Therefore  

   P² = 308 + (676√5 – 308) = 676√5.

5.  Write P² in the required form m√n with n square-free:  

m = 676, n = 5.

Hence  

m + n = 676 + 5 = 681.

Let the sides of the (convex) equiangular pentagon, in order, be  
a, b, c, d, e.  
All interior angles are 108°, so successive side‐vectors make a constant external turn of 72°.

1.  Vector relations  
   Write the side–vectors as  
   vₖ = sₖ uₖ, uₖ = e^{i kθ}, θ = 72°, k = 0,…,4, s₀=a, s₁=b,…  
   The pentagon closes: Σ vₖ = 0.

2.  Diagonal lengths  
   The diagonal joining vertices k and k+2 is v_{k+1}+v_{k+2}.  
   Its squared length:  
   d_k² = s_{k+1}² + s_{k+2}² + 2 s_{k+1}s_{k+2} cos 72°.

   Summing all five diagonals,

        Σ d_k² = 2 Σ s_k² + 2 cos 72° Σ s_k s_{k+1}.

   Given Σ s_k² = 308 and Σ d_k² = 800, with cos 72° = (√5−1)/4,

        616 + (√5−1)/2 · T = 800 where T = Σ s_k s_{k+1}  
        ⇒ T = 92(√5 + 1).

3.  Using the closure condition  
   0 = |Σ v_k|² = Σ s_k² + 2 cos 72° T + 2 cos 144° U,
